review_scope: Coordinator adjudicated every complete composed answer against primary source contexts; all three episodes read in full. Same-team development review, not external blind benchmark. Runtime context and exact answer snapshots checked separately.

cases.question: Which Star Wars game did Johnny call his favorite, and why?
cases.query: Super Empire Strikes Back favorite lightsaber Force
cases.answer: In this episode Johnny answers Super Empire Strikes Back without hesitation. He connects it with his favorite Star Wars film and the satisfaction of having force moves and a lightsaber, recalling wanting a good Star Wars game with his cousin. That is his stated preference here, not Kat's favorite or proof his opinion never changed.
cases.reason: P29–30 directly support Johnny's episode-specific Super Empire preference and remembered rationale.

cases.question: Did either host actually play Battle for Naboo, and how should its comments be used?
cases.query: Battle for Naboo Nimbu never played box
cases.answer: Neither host claims to have played it: Kat names it as her unplayed N64 entry and Johnny says he has not played it at all. Johnny's contribution is limited to having seen video and finding its box difficult to locate in good condition, alongside a dated relative-rarity claim. This is not a firsthand gameplay verdict or a verified current rarity ranking.
cases.reason: Both hosts deny Naboo play; video/box observations remain separate from firsthand review.

cases.question: What happened to Johnny's Masters of Teräs Käsi copies?
cases.query: Masters Teres Kazi day one lent re-bought
cases.answer: Johnny reports buying the game day one and playing it in his military dorm. He later lent that copy out and never saw it again, then says he bought another for about five dollars. These are a first purchase, an unreturned loan and a later replacement—not a sale, a recovered loaned copy, or a verified exact purchase date.
cases.reason: P23–24 support first purchase, lost loan and replacement; no returned original or exact calendar date.

cases.question: What Sega-platform correction and game-name correction should the lore preserve?
cases.query: Sega CD correct myself Vigilante Racer Vigilante 8
cases.answer: Johnny initially describes a Sega landscape dominated by Game Gear and 32X, then immediately adds Sega CD and Rebel Assault, including a 3DO version. Separately, he first calls Demolition's comparator Vigilante Racer, then checks and confirms Vigilante 8. The false start should remain correction history, not a second game identity or evidence that Sega CD had no Star Wars games.
forbidden: Vigilante Racer is another identified game
cases.reason: Sega CD omission and Vigilante 8 correction retained, without treating false starts as true separate games.

cases.question: Was Johnny's Star Wars checklist already complete and published?
cases.query: checklist comprehensive accessories work in process
cases.answer: No completed publication is established. Johnny says he is revising earlier inaccuracies, has finished the Nintendo portion, and may post the document even while incomplete. He later explicitly says accessory coverage will not be comprehensive and invites missing items. The ambitious comprehensive language must be read with those limits, not as an accepted exhaustive inventory.
cases.reason: Checklist aspirations qualified by incomplete platform/accessory work and uncertain future posting.

cases.question: What had Johnny and Kat actually played that day, versus only planned to try?
cases.query: played today Super Star Wars Shadow another go Leia
cases.answer: Johnny says he played through Super Star Wars that day and has been playing unspecified Battlefront intermittently. Kat says she gave Shadows of the Empire another go and still did not love it. Johnny may try the Game Gear Star Wars Leia level but explicitly has never played it; Kat likewise wants to try the 32X game she has never played. These future possibilities are not purchases or completed playthroughs.
forbidden: Kat played the Game Gear Leia level
All SNES trilogy games completed that day
cases.reason: P29–30 distinguish actual Super Star Wars/Battlefront/Shadows play from Leia-level/32X intentions.

cases.question: Does the 32X NFR make another Star Wars game, and do Infinity figures count as games?
cases.query: NFR variant Disney Infinity 19 50
cases.answer: Johnny treats the 32X Star Wars Arcade NFR as a variant and tentatively describes it as a pack-in; Virtua Fighter is the other named NFR example, not another Star Wars title. The Disney Infinity discussion separately distinguishes about nineteen individual figures from about fifty variants plus starter/bundle configurations. Those are dated collectible-product counts, not fifty different video games or a current verified catalog.
forbidden: NFR is a new underlying game
cases.reason: NFR remains edition variant; Infinity figures/variants are collectible products, not fifty video games.

cases.question: What does the episode actually support about the NES, Master System and Game Gear Star Wars versions?
cases.query: Master System Nintendo Game Gear exclusive Leia
cases.answer: Johnny corrects his wording to call Master System Star Wars basically the Nintendo version, then says the Game Gear port adds an exclusive Leia level involving plans for R2. That supports a source-reported port-family link while preserving platform and content differences. It does not verify identical code, establish the Game Boy version as the same game, or prove Johnny had played the Leia level.
cases.reason: P10 source-reported NES/Master System/Game Gear link qualified; P29 confirms Leia nonplay.

cases.question: Did Johnny finally buy the Monster in My Pocket figure?
cases.query: Monster Pocket figure hundred box
cases.answer: No acquisition is reported. Johnny says he opened his box after the earlier episode hoping the figure had been overlooked, but it was not there. They mention a roughly $100 eBay listing; that is an asking opportunity, not his payment or receipt.
cases.reason: P3–5 explicitly retain missing figurine and listing rather than payment.

cases.question: Which coffin items did Kat and Tyler choose, and did they own them?

cases.answer: Kat chooses the Splatterhouse PS3 press kit, describing a steel coffin, soundtrack and mask, and says she would like it. Tyler chooses Darkwatch's wooden coffin edition, reporting a forum-point acquisition system and an uncertain badge. Neither account establishes ownership. Darkwatch's 22,000-point cost and the highest member's 20,226 points are reported research, not a verified sale price.
cases.reason: Coffin picks and wants are not ownership; points are historical reported research, not dollars.

cases.question: Who wanted the Resident Evil4 chainsaw controller and who already had it?
cases.query: Resident Evil chainsaw Kat GameCube

This should not become a positive preference claim, just as the Life Is Strange callback is not reliable evidence she enjoyed that game.

cases.reason: P35–36 preserve Johnny's liked/disliked pinball experiences and disagreement without purchase inference.

cases.query: What were Tyler’s two early Japanese computer purchases and why did the more obscure one cost more?
cases.answer: Tyler received first-release PC-88 Nobunaga’s Ambition after a two-year search, paying about $150 and assembling three different forms including a floppy-folder variant. From the same seller he also bought Hoi Hoi, paying about two to three times as much after Tiger Wolf’s encouragement. Hoi Hoi’s relevance to his genre-history collection supplied the reason: it is discussed as an early Stop That Roach antecedent with a hex grid, unlike the Game Boy game’s grid-based turn puzzle. These are dated purchase reports, not proof Hoi Hoi has a particular global print count.
forbidden: Do not substitute Kid Dracula for either of these two linked computer buys.
Do not claim exact Hoi Hoi paid total, print count, or identical Game Boy release.
cases.reason: Full source 01:23:52–01:26:55 supports the two linked computer purchases, approximate relative price, three versions and genre-history rationale; no global rarity certification.

forbidden: Do not call sample cartridge an authenticated prototype.
Do not attribute first-hand Game Boy play to Tyler.

Do not infer a replacement order or verified compatibility of all components.

cases.answer: No single objective winner is established. Tyler says he owns around twelve Myst copies, so his preference for Doom is not proof he dislikes or does not collect Myst. Half-Life is another answer Tyler accepts, while Zork receives a relevance objection.
